A rare recessive ataxic disorder is identified in several unrelated families. Patient-derived Purkinje neurons (from iPSC differentiation) show the following consistent abnormalities.

Normal passive membrane properties and resting potential, but a significantly increased input resistance during sustained depolarization, without changes in \({Na^+}\) or \({K^+}\) conductances.

Climbing-fiber–evoked \({Ca}^{2+}\) spikes are normal in amplitude but decay nearly twice as slowly, accompanied by prolonged after hyperpolarization.

Parallel-fiber long-term depression (LTD) and rebound potentiation are both intact, yet climbing-fiber–evoked complex spikes show progressive broadening during trains at \(1\) Hz.

Normal expression of \({Cav2.1}\), \({IP3R1}\), \({SERCA2}\), and \({calbindin-D28k}\); however, high-resolution immuno-EM shows selective mislocalization of \({Ca}^{2+}\)-ATPase pumps and \({Na^+}\)/\({Ca}^{2+}\) exchangers away from distal dendritic spines and toward the soma.

Reveals marked downregulation of a single ER–plasma membrane tethering protein, which normally binds \({VAPB}\) and \({ORAI1}\), coupling store-operated \({Ca}^{2+}\) entry to local microdomain refilling in Purkinje dendrites.

Which single molecular target best explains this pattern of mislocalized \({Ca}^{2+}\) signaling and abnormal Purkinje dendritic excitability?

Consider a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator in the presence of a time-dependent external force, that is, a driven harmonic oscillator with Hamiltonian  
\(H = \dfrac{p^{2}}{2m} + \dfrac{m\omega^{2}}{2}x^{2} - x\,F(t).\)

The propagator \(K_{F}(x',x;t_{f},t_{i})\) describing the motion from position \(x\) at the initial time \(t_{i}\) to position \(x'\) at the final time \(t_{f}\) can be expressed in terms of the classical action. After a direct but lengthy calculation, it is found that  
\(K_{F}(x',x;t_{f},t_{i}) = K(x',x;T)\,e^{iX/\hbar},\)  
where \(T=t_{f}-t_{i}\) and \(K(x',x;T)\) is the propagator of the unperturbed harmonic oscillator.

The phase factor \(X\) is given by  
\(X = \dfrac{J_{3}}{4m\omega} - \dfrac{J_{1}J_{2} - 2x'm\omega J_{1} - 2xm\omega J_{2}}{2m\omega\sin\omega T}.\)

The quantities \(J_{1}\), \(J_{2}\), and \(J_{3}\) are defined through the integrals  
\(J_{1} = \int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} dt\,F(t)\sin\omega(t-t_{i}),\)  
\(J_{2} = \int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} dt\,F(t)\sin\omega(t_{f}-t),\)  
and  
\(J_{3} = \int_{t_{i}}^{t_{f}} dt\,F(t)\int_{t_{i}}^{t} dt'\,F(t')\sin\omega(t-t').\)

The unperturbed harmonic oscillator propagator is  
\(K(x',x;T) = \sqrt{\dfrac{m\omega}{2\pi i\hbar\sin\omega T}}\,
\exp\!\left[\dfrac{i m\omega}{2\hbar}
\left((x^{2}+x'^{2})\cot\omega T - \dfrac{2xx'}{\sin\omega T}\right)\right].\)

Assume that initially, at time \(t=t_{i}\), the system is in its ground state. At a later time \(t_{0}>t_{i}\), the system is subjected to the instantaneous force discussed above. Calculate the probability of finding the system again in the ground state at some later time \(t_{f}>t_{0}\). You may use the matrix elements  
\(\langle n|e^{ikx}|0\rangle = \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{n!}} \exp\!\left(-\dfrac{\hbar k^{2}}{2m\omega}\right)\left(i k\sqrt{\dfrac{\hbar}{2m\omega}}\right)^{n}.\)

The coefficients are uniquely determined by the oscillator dynamics as  
\(\gamma=\dfrac{\sin\omega(t_{f}-t_{0})\sin\omega(t_{0}-t_{i})}{\sin\omega(t_{f}-t_{i})},\)  
\(\alpha=\dfrac{\sin\omega(t_{0}-t_{i})}{\sin\omega(t_{f}-t_{i})},\)  
and  
\(\beta=\dfrac{\sin\omega(t_{f}-t_{0})}{\sin\omega(t_{f}-t_{i})}.\)

Assumptions:

1. The system is a one-dimensional harmonic oscillator with fixed mass and angular frequency.

2. The external force acts instantaneously at a single time and is represented by a Dirac delta function.

3. The impulse delivered by the force is finite and corresponds to a definite momentum transfer to the system.

4. The time ordering satisfies that the impulse occurs strictly between the initial and final times of propagation.

5. The general expression for the driven harmonic oscillator propagator is valid for arbitrary time-dependent forces.

6. The propagator of the unperturbed harmonic oscillator is known exactly and is used without approximation.

7. The quantum evolution of the system is unitary, so the effect of the impulse appears only as a phase factor in the propagator.

8. No additional interactions, damping, or environmental effects are present; the oscillator is otherwise isolated.
